title: China details its path to a crewed Moon landing before 2030 - NASASpaceFlight.com
html:
China has set out its most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon before 2030, with three uncrewed missions planned before China’s first crew to leave Earth orbit will attempt the country’s first lunar landing. The lunar program builds on China’s continuing experience with the Tiangong space station, which prepares for its next crew rotation this month, including its first foreign visitor, one of two candidates from Pakistan.

China first officially announced its crewed lunar landing plans at the Shenzhou-16 pre-launch press conference in Jiuquan on May 29, 2023. Lin Xiqiang, then Deputy Director and spokesperson for the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), set the goal for the first Chinese landing “by 2030”, which would see two crewmembers spending around six hours on the surface, while a third waited in orbit.

Render of the Chinese lunar lander on the Moon, as envisioned in 2023 (Credit: CMSA)

Some additional details around the Chang Zheng 10 architecture followed six weeks later during the 9th China (International) Commercial Aerospace Forum in Wuhan. This included more information about the hardware that would be used to execute China’s goal, including the crewed ship, lander, and rover, with plans for an Apollo-style lunar orbit rendezvous (LOR).

This year, the agency used the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing, which began on Oct. 31, to present a more detailed plan around mission sequencing. The conference brought together more than 800 experts across the two days, with 15 sub-forums covering three key themes of common technologies, the Tiangong space station and lunar exploration.

There are some similarities to the Apollo missions, once in lunar orbit. The Mengzhou (“Dream Vessel”) crewed spacecraft will meet up with the Lanyue (“Embracing the Moon”) lander, which will already be waiting in orbit. Two of the crew will descend to the surface, while a third remains aboard Mengzhou to monitor and support. The lander will spend three days on the Moon, with the crew potentially conducting daily extravehicular activities (EVAs). They will then ascend in the lander and dock again with the Mengzhou craft, which will separate and return the crew home.

The Wangyu (“gazing at the cosmos”) lunar suit was unveiled in September 2024 and named in February 2025, following a public naming contest (Credit: CMSA)

Straight to the surface

Unlike the Apollo or Artemis programs, however, the first time a Chinese crew will visit the Moon will be for the first crewed landing attempt. There are no equivalents to the Apollo 8 or 10 missions, and no crewed docking test in low-Earth orbit (LEO) analogous to Artemis III.

China plans to leverage what it has learned from the robotic Chang’e missions, which have already proven autonomous lunar ascent and lunar orbit docking on both 2020’s Chang’e 5 and 2024’s Chang’e 6 missions. A series of three uncrewed Mengzhou missions are also planned before the first crewed landing attempt.

First, a single-core Chang Zheng 10A (CZ-10A) will send an uncrewed Mengzhou craft to the Tiangong space station. Dubbed Mengzhou-1, this mission has slipped from 2026 and is now expected in early 2027. The CZ-10A has been designed specifically for carrying Mengzhou to the station, and features a reusable first stage (shared with the CZ-10B) and the capability to lift between 14,000 and 18,000 kg into LEO. This flight will carry cargo to the station and will validate Mengzhou’s orbital operations, in particular docking, as well as demonstrating its subsequent re-entry. Subsequent missions to the station may also be planned outside the scope of the lunar program.

Render of the Chang Zheng 10 (Credit: CCTV)

The second uncrewed flight will use a single Chang Zheng 10 (CZ-10) to loft an uncrewed Lanyue lander, which will travel to the Moon to demonstrate landing and ascent, likely in 2028. The CZ-10 is a triple-core heavy lift vehicle, capable of carrying around 27,000 kg to trans-lunar injection (TLI).

The final uncrewed mission, which is expected around 2029, will use a pair of CZ-10 launches – the same profile planned for crewed missions – with one carrying Mengzhou and the other Lanyue. These will conduct a full end-to-end robotic dress rehearsal of the lunar mission. As much of the mission as possible will be practiced, including TLI, lunar orbit insertion, docking, landing and surface operations, ascent and re-docking, and Mengzhou’s return trip.

Assuming the uncrewed tests are completed successfully, the next mission will carry a crew to repeat the same mission profile and become China’s first astronauts to walk on the Moon. This may be planned to coincide with the 80th anniversary year of the People’s Republic of China, should it take place in 2029. Later missions will grow in length to around 14 days, or one lunar daylight period.

Illustration of a potential future Chinese lunar base with the support of the Queqiao-2 satellite (Credit: CAST)

Lunar exploration project

Wang Xiang is Deputy Chief Designer of China’s human spaceflight program and Chief Designer of the newly merged Lunar Exploration Project. He presented these lunar plans on Oct. 31. The CMSA had announced in May this year that the crewed landing program and the robotic Chang’e program had been merged into this single project.

Wang outlined two planning principles. Anything to be done in lunar orbit will first be verified in “near-Earth orbit”, using the Tiangong station wherever possible. Additionally, anything involving crew will first be flown uncrewed wherever possible. Only once the basic technologies of the CZ-10A and Mengzhou’s re-entry and recovery are proven, will the CZ-10 launch the lunar Mengzhou.

During each mission, the Lanyue lander will launch ahead of the crew and loiter in lunar orbit for the arrival of the Mengzhou craft. This two-launch architecture, in which the two spacecraft “shake hands” in lunar orbit, leverages existing technical capabilities, Wang noted. Developing Mengzhou and Lanyue separately also allows each to evolve into a standardized family of variants for long-term use, including versions for LEO and lunar missions.

Render of Mengzhou and Lanyue spacecraft approaching to dock (Credit: CCTV/CMSA)

Mengzhou is already following this path with two variants. The lunar version has four engines and full-size tanks, whereas the LEO version has two engines and smaller tanks, while retaining the same service module form factor. With a mass of around 26,000 kg, it fits just within its carrier rocket’s maximum payload capacity.

Similarly, cargo, rover, and habitat-module versions of the Lanyue lander are under consideration. The two-stage Lanyue also has a total mass of around 26,000 kg. This consists of a propulsion stage, which is jettisoned during descent, and a landing module whose mass is between 9,000 and 10,000 kg. This utilizes four variable-thrust YF-36 engines derived from the Chang’e family, as well as a new high-thrust pump-fed engine, thought to be the YF-58, which was tested in Tongchuan.

The uncrewed lander will collect essential environmental data on site, including lunar surface temperature and dust conditions, as well as recording the spacecraft’s in-flight performance. These will help to define the temperatures and dust conditions that the Wangyu lunar suits, the Tansuo rover and Lanyue’s own systems will need to cope with during the crew’s planned three-day stay on the surface.

Lanyue lander testing in Hebei Province, August 2025 (Credit: CGTN/CMG)

The rehearsal missions will deliver valuable performance data on how the lander behaves during descent, on the surface and during ascent. This will build upon data gathered during the landing and takeoff tests that were conducted at Huailai in Hebei Province in 2025. The facility, which was built to test the Chang’e landers, uses tall towers and cables to simulate one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, and has been described as Asia’s largest test site for landing on extraterrestrial bodies.

The CMSA invited active Chinese experimental payloads to potentially benefit from a “free ride” on the uncrewed Lanyue mission, provided they meet a limit of 50 kg in mass and 100 W in power consumption. “Since we are not carrying a crew we will have some surplus resources, and we want to make full and eﬀective use of them”, Wang noted, adding that the agency will select some meaningful scientific experiments to be conducted on the Moon during the mission.

Another notable difference between China’s plans and the Apollo missions is the intent to carry the Tansuo rover on the first landing. NASA only used its Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) on the final three Apollo missions, beginning with Apollo 15 in 1971. Tansuo is currently in the prototype development phase, and the final rover is expected to weigh about 200 kg. It will carry two astronauts, together with experiment and sampling hardware, within a 10 km range of the landing site.

Mengzhou conducts its in-flight abort demonstration (Credit: CNSA)

Mengzhou completed its zero-altitude pad abort testing in June 2025, later demonstrating an abort during flight at Max-Q (the point of maximum aerodynamic pressure on the vehicle) during a low-altitude flight test on Feb.11, 2026. The mission also demonstrated the first stage booster that forms a key part of the CZ-10 architecture. This made a controlled splashdown alongside the Linghangzhe catch ship during the abort test mission. The CZ-10A and CZ-10 rockets are yet to make their debut flights.

The CZ-10 owes much to the heritage of the Chang Zheng 5 (CZ-5), which has been China’s heaviest-lift launcher since entering service in 2016. In that time, it has carried out a number of high-profile missions, including sending the Tianwen-1 spacecraft to Mars, the Chang’e-5 and Chang’e-6 sample-return missions to the Moon, and deploying the modular Tiangong station into LEO. Early concepts for the CZ-10 used the designation Chang Zheng 5G.

Both rockets are built by the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology around 5-meter-diameter cores, enabling the CZ-10 to reuse existing manufacturing and handling infrastructure. At roughly 92 m tall, the CZ-10 dwarfs the shorter 57 m CZ-5, while it has three 5-meter cores each powered by seven YF-100K engines, compared to the CZ-5’s single core flanked by four smaller side boosters.

Illustration for scale of the Chang Zheng 10 family, its Chang Zheng 5 heritage and the Chang Zheng 2F/G currently launching crew to the Tiangong station.

Landing location and lunar base

While NASA’s Artemis IV mission is targeting a landing near the lunar south pole, China is expected to pick a lower-latitude site on the near side of the Moon, which will enhance safety and facilitate easier communications and access to solar power. Rimae Bode is currently the leading candidate amongst 14 potential sites that are being reviewed from an initial selection of 106. Located just north of the lunar equator, near the Sinus Aestuum volcanic plains, it offers relatively flat terrain.

Longer-term plans include the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), which was announced in 2021 as a joint project with Russia. With China now leading the project, assembly of a basic station at the lunar south pole is targeted for 2035, while Russia will deliver a nuclear power plant for the station by 2036.

Following the failure of its Luna-25 mission in August 2023, Russia has delayed the robotic Luna-26 mission to around 2027-2028 and has no plans for crewed lunar expeditions before 2036. Thirteen nations have signed up as ILRS partners, including Thailand, Senegal, and Serbia, who are also amongst the 78 signatories of NASA’s Artemis Accords to date.

Renders of the mobile lunar laboratory and habitat concepts shown in 2023 and 2026 respectively (Credit: CMSA)

CMSA officials have increasingly leaned towards initially using roving labs rather than a permanent fixed base, while China builds its lunar experience ahead of a longer-term ILRS presence. Future variations on the modular Lanyue family include cargo and night-capable versions, plus a laboratory rover, which was first unveiled in July 2023 in Wuhan.

This pressurized rover takes the place of the crew cabin on the lander, and could be used to explore the surface autonomously or with crew aboard. Several rovers can be joined together, or to a Lanyue lander, to create larger habitable volumes. CMSA deputy chief designer Zhang Hailian described it as a large-range mobile lab which can support short crew stays and develop into a “lunar research and test station”.

Mission patches for the Mengzhou abort test, two of the final selections for the Mengzhou-1 mission, and Shenzhou-24 (Credit: CMSA)

Shenzhou-24 mission

While China plans to land astronauts on the moon by the end of the decade, its human spaceflight program is currently focused on the Tiangong space station in low-Earth orbit. The station is currently served by the Shenzhou spacecraft and, later this month, will welcome its next crew rotation. Shenzhou-24 is currently anticipated to launch no earlier than Nov. 25.

As well as carrying two Chinese astronauts for the next long-duration stay aboard Tiangong, it will also be carrying the first Pakistani astronaut to reach orbit. The CMSA has not yet named the crew, but Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud have both been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing since April this year.

The Pakistani astronaut will become the first foreign national to visit the station, staying aboard for about a week while the crew handover takes place, before returning aboard Shenzhou-23 with two members of the station’s current crew. One of the current crew, Zhu Yangzhu, Li Jiaying, or Zhang Zhiyuan, will stay aboard for a further six months, becoming China’s first astronaut to spend a continuous year in orbit. The crew has recently been conducting brain function research, amongst other sensory experiments relating to prolonged stays in microgravity, as they approach the end of their expedition.

(Lead image: Render of the Mengzhou and Lanyue spacecraft docking in lunar orbit – Credit: CMSA/CCTV)
summary: China has set out its most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon…
